strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: replacing a single globally-fused 3D point cloud (which accumulates cross-view misalignment) with multiple per-frame local geometric memories avoids ghosting/drift artifacts and is well illustrated in Fig. 1.

The coverage-driven retrieval formulation (greedy visibility-coverage maximization) is a sensible and clearly specified algorithmic contribution (Algorithm 1), addressing redundancy and completeness of anchor selection.

The multi-anchor weaving controller (shared cross-anchor attention + pose-guided fusion) is a reasonable architectural design to reconcile residual misalignment across multiple noisy anchors rather than simply averaging or ignoring it, and the ablations (Fig. 5, Table 2/3) support each design choice individually (global vs local memory, joint vs separate attention, pose-guided fusion vs averaging, number of retrieved anchors).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: quantitative comparison against many recent strong baselines (Gen3C, TrajCrafter, ViewCrafter, SEVA, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on two datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV) with both reconstruction fidelity (PSNR/SSIM) and VBench perceptual metrics, plus camera-controllability comparison (Table 4) and generalization to two backbones (CogVideoX, Wan2.2).

Good faith effort at reproducibility/fairness: baselines without public code (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) were reimplemented on the same backbone and training data, and implementation details (chunk sizes, training steps, optimizer, GPU count) are provided in the appendix.

Extensive qualitative results including open-domain, long-horizon (up to 241 frames), 360-degree panoramic, and even out-of-distribution third-person dynamic-character scenarios, showing practical value of the method beyond the narrow training distribution.
weaknesses: The improvement over the strongest baseline (SEVA) in consistency scores is modest/comparable per Table 1 (PSNR 21.13 vs 21.04, similar SSIM), and the main claimed gains are largely in perceptual/quality metrics (VBench) rather than a decisive advantage in geometric consistency, which is the paper's central claim; this could be discussed more critically rather than framed as clearly superior.

The evaluation setting (partial-revisit with 49 target / 21 history frames sampled from existing video datasets) is relatively controlled; true long-horizon consistency (hundreds of frames, many chunks, error accumulation over many retrieve-generate iterations) is only shown qualitatively (Figs. 6, 12) without quantitative metrics (e.g., no PSNR/consistency scores reported for the multi-segment/241-frame generations), leaving open how much drift accumulates over very long horizons.

Reliance on a single off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction/pose estimator (TTT3R) for constructing local memories is not stress-tested — there is no ablation on sensitivity to the underlying geometry/pose estimator quality, which is central to the method's robustness claims in challenging or textureless scenes.

Computational overhead (rendering multiple anchors per chunk, running a per-frame 3D estimator, shared multi-anchor attention with K up to 4-6x more tokens) is not quantified — no discussion of inference latency, memory footprint, or scalability of the memory bank as videos grow arbitrarily long, which matters for the claimed long-horizon use case.

Some baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are reimplemented by the authors rather than using official released weights/results, which, despite the stated fairness rationale, introduces potential risk of suboptimal baseline tuning that is difficult for readers to independently verify.

The paper's contribution is primarily a systems-style integration of existing ideas (per-frame local point clouds instead of global fusion, greedy coverage retrieval, ControlNet-style multi-condition fusion with attention) rather than a fundamentally new technique; novelty is somewhat incremental relative to concurrent contemporaneous works (SPMem, Spatia, MagicWorld) cited as closest related work, though the paper does differentiate itself reasonably.

strengths: Clearly identifies a real and well-motivated limitation of prior memory-augmented video generation work: fusing multi-view observations into a single global 3D point cloud accumulates cross-view misalignment (pose/depth errors), which propagates into rendered anchors and causes hallucinated/ghosted content. Replacing this with a collection of clean per-frame local point clouds is a sensible and intuitively justified design choice.

The coverage-driven retrieval formulation (greedy visibility-coverage maximization with FoV pre-filtering) is clearly specified, including a full algorithm listing in the appendix, making the retrieval strategy reasonably reproducible.

The multi-anchor weaving controller (shared multi-anchor attention + pose-guided importance fusion) is well ablated: Table 2 isolates the benefit of local vs. global memory, Table 3 the effect of number of retrieved anchors, and Figure 5 the effect of pose-guided fusion vs. naive averaging and joint vs. separate attention, providing reasonably convincing evidence that each component contributes.

Experiments are conducted across two different DiT backbones (CogVideoX and Wan2.2), and quantitative comparisons are made against a fairly comprehensive set of recent baselines (Gen3C, TrajCrafter, ViewCrafter, SEVA, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem), several of which were carefully reimplemented for fair comparison under identical retrieval/anchor settings.

Qualitative results are extensive, including free-form keyboard-controlled trajectories, open-domain generalization beyond the training distribution, 360° panoramic exploration, and zero-shot third-person dynamic-character scenarios, which support the claimed generality of the approach beyond the narrow train/eval distribution.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is restricted to RealEstate10K and DL3DV, both largely static, real-estate/indoor-style scenes with a 70-frame partial-revisit protocol (49 target frames); the more ambitious long-horizon claims (up to 241 frames, 360° revisits, dynamic third-person scenes) are demonstrated only qualitatively, so the paper's central 'long-horizon world consistency' claim is not quantitatively substantiated beyond a relatively short horizon.

The method's local memories depend entirely on an external per-frame 3D reconstruction model (TTT3R); while per-frame geometry avoids cross-view fusion drift, per-frame scale/depth errors and their propagation through retrieval/rendering are not analyzed, and no failure-case or sensitivity analysis with respect to the underlying 3D estimator is provided.

No discussion of computational overhead: retrieving and rendering up to K anchors per chunk plus a multi-anchor controller with shared attention across K anchor videos is inherently more expensive (memory and runtime) than single global-memory conditioning, yet no timing/memory footprint comparison against baselines is given, which matters for practical adoption in long-horizon generation.

Handling of dynamic content is ad hoc (masking the moving character out of the point-cloud memory) and only demonstrated in one zero-shot example; the approach's applicability to scenes with substantial non-rigid or multiple dynamic elements is unclear and not evaluated.

Several strong baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are not open-sourced and were reimplemented by the authors, raising some risk that these reimplementations may be under-tuned relative to the original works, which could inflate the apparent margin of improvement.

The paper lacks an explicit Limitations section discussing failure modes (e.g., retrieval failures when no local memory provides sufficient coverage, degradation with very sparse historical context, or scaling of the memory bank size over arbitrarily long trajectories), which would be valuable given the long-horizon, memory-accumulating nature of the proposed system.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification: global 3D reconstruction/fusion accumulates cross-view misalignment that propagates into hallucinated/ghosted content in rendered anchor videos; the paper diagnoses this failure mode convincingly with Figure 1.

The core idea of replacing a single globally fused 3D memory with a collection of clean per-frame local point clouds is simple, well-motivated, and effectively avoids fusion-induced drift/ghosting artifacts.

The coverage-driven retrieval formulation (greedy visibility-coverage maximization with FoV candidate filtering) is clearly specified and reduces redundant/irrelevant memories; a full algorithm listing is provided in the appendix for reproducibility.

The multi-anchor weaving controller (shared cross-anchor attention + pose-guided importance fusion) is a nontrivial architectural contribution that meaningfully reconciles residual misalignment among multiple imperfect anchors rather than assuming perfect geometry.

Extensive empirical validation: two different DiT backbones (CogVideoX, Wan2.2), comparisons against seven recent strong baselines (Gen3C, TrajCrafter, ViewCrafter, SEVA, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on two datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV), plus VBench-based perceptual metrics and reconstruction metrics.

Thorough and well-designed ablations isolating the contribution of each component: global vs. local memory (Table 2), pose-guided fusion vs. averaging and joint vs. separate attention (Figure 5), and the effect of retrieval budget K (Table 3).

Additional camera-controllability evaluation (rotation/translation error, Table 4) and demonstration of generalization to long-horizon (241-frame), 360° panoramic, and zero-shot dynamic third-person scenarios not seen during training, indicating good potential impact and robustness beyond the training distribution.
Reasonably detailed implementation and baseline-reimplementation descriptions in the appendix support reproducibility given the method's reliance on non-open-sourced baselines.
weaknesses: Two baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are reimplemented by the authors since official code is unavailable; while this is disclosed and reasonable, it introduces potential asymmetry in tuning quality that is hard for readers to fully verify.

No analysis of inference-time/computational overhead: the pipeline requires per-frame 3D estimation (TTT3R), coverage-based retrieval search, and rendering/encoding of up to K anchor videos per chunk, but runtime, memory, and scalability comparisons against baselines are not reported.

Quantitative improvements over the strongest baseline (SEVA) are mixed rather than uniformly dominant — e.g., SEVA achieves a comparable or slightly better PSNR (21.13 vs. 21.04) — so the overall superiority claim rests more on aggregate quality/consistency scores than a clean sweep across all metrics.

The method still depends on an external per-frame 3D reconstruction estimator (TTT3R); while fusion-induced errors are avoided, no analysis is given of how errors in the underlying per-frame pose/depth estimates (which are not corrected by avoiding fusion) affect the local memories and downstream generation quality.

Limited discussion of AnchorWeave's own failure modes/limitations (e.g., behavior when candidate memory pools provide little coverage, or in highly dynamic scenes); most failure-mode discussion is devoted to baselines rather than the proposed method.
No human/user study is included to corroborate the automated VBench-based perceptual quality claims, which would strengthen the case for genuinely improved visual quality beyond metric numbers.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem framing: existing global 3D memory fusion for camera-controllable video generation accumulates cross-view misalignment that propagates into hallucinated/ghosted content; the paper diagnoses this clearly (Fig. 1) and proposes a principled alternative.

Technically coherent solution combining three complementary components: per-frame local geometric memories (avoiding fusion drift), coverage-driven greedy retrieval that maximizes visibility coverage along the target trajectory, and a multi-anchor weaving controller (shared cross-anchor attention + pose-guided importance fusion) that reconciles residual misalignment across multiple anchors.

Extensive quantitative evaluation against many recent, relevant baselines (Gen3C, SEVA, ViewCrafter, TrajCrafter, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on RealEstate10K and DL3DV, with consistent improvements across reconstruction fidelity (PSNR/SSIM) and VBench-style perceptual metrics, and consistent gains on two different DiT backbones (CogVideoX, Wan2.2).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each design choice: global vs. local memory (Table 2), pose-guided vs. naive averaging fusion, joint vs. separate attention (Fig. 5), and effect of retrieval budget K (Table 3), each supported by both quantitative numbers and qualitative visualizations.

Rich supplementary analyses beyond the main claims: efficiency/scaling comparison showing sub-linear cost growth versus SPMem's global-fusion approach (Fig. 8), a demanding 2400-frame explore-and-revisit stress test showing much better long-term consistency than the closest global-memory baseline (Fig. 10), camera-controllability comparison (Table 5), and candid discussion of failure modes (reflective surfaces) and limitations.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed implementation/training hyperparameters, retrieval algorithm pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and description of baseline reimplementation procedures.

Demonstrated generalization to open-domain, zero-shot scenarios (keyboard-controlled long-horizon exploration, 360° panoramic consistency, and even dynamic third-person character scenes via masking) despite training only on static real-estate/scene datasets.
weaknesses: No human perceptual study is included; conclusions about visual quality and consistency rely entirely on automated metrics (PSNR/SSIM, VBench dimensions) and qualitative figures selected by the authors, which can be susceptible to selection bias.

Several baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are not open-sourced and had to be reimplemented by the authors for comparison; while described in detail, this raises some risk of implementation mismatch or suboptimal tuning that could bias the comparison in the proposed method's favor.

The approach still depends on an off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction/pose estimator (TTT3R); its own pose/depth errors are not eliminated, only prevented from being fused into a single distorted global map. The long-horizon stress test (Fig. 10) shows performance still gradually degrades after ~1000 frames due to accumulated synthesis errors and pose drift written back into memory, indicating the core misalignment problem is mitigated rather than solved.

Multi-anchor conditioning adds non-trivial runtime and memory overhead relative to a single-anchor baseline (275s vs 221s, 39GB vs 34GB GPU memory at K=4 per Table 4), which may limit applicability in latency- or memory-constrained settings despite favorable scaling versus the global-fusion baseline.

Dynamic content handling relies on a manual/heuristic masking strategy to exclude moving objects from the static memory, and the proposed extension for tracking out-of-sight dynamic entities (Fig. 12) is only sketched conceptually rather than being an integrated, evaluated component of the system.

Evaluation is restricted to two DiT-based video diffusion backbones and largely indoor/real-estate-style scene datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV); broader architectural or domain diversity (e.g., outdoor driving, highly dynamic scenes) is not systematically evaluated within the quantitative benchmark.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the paper identifies a concrete failure mode of existing global-3D-memory video generation methods (cross-view misalignment accumulating into noisy fused geometry) and illustrates it convincingly in Figure 1.

The core idea of replacing a single globally-fused memory with multiple per-frame local geometric memories, combined with coverage-driven retrieval and a learned multi-anchor weaving controller, is a reasonable and technically sound way to sidestep fusion-induced artifacts while still exploiting explicit 3D structure.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons against six strong, recent camera-controllable/memory-augmented baselines (Gen3C, SEVA, ViewCrafter, TrajCrafter, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on two datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV), with both reconstruction metrics (PSNR/SSIM) and VBench-style perceptual metrics.
Thorough ablation studies (global vs. local memory, pose-guided vs. average fusion, joint vs. separate attention, number of retrievals K) that individually support the design choices.

Substantial appendix material, including a dedicated diagnostic experiment quantifying degradation of global point-cloud fusion (44.93→16.15 dB after 45 frames), a 2400-frame long-horizon revisit stress test against SPMem, runtime/memory scaling analysis, camera-controllability comparison (rotation/translation error), and an explicit failure-mode discussion (reflective surfaces, pose drift, backbone dependence).

Demonstrated generalization to open-domain, keyboard-controlled long-horizon exploration and even zero-shot third-person dynamic scenes despite training only on static datasets, which is a meaningful practical result.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the explicitly cited closest prior works (SPMem, Context-as-Memory, Spatia): the main new ingredients are a coverage-driven retrieval heuristic and an attention/pose-weighted anchor-fusion controller layered on otherwise standard ControlNet-style anchor-video conditioning; the paper itself frames its contribution largely as "replace global fusion with retrieval over local memories," which is a fairly direct combination of existing retrieval-augmented-memory and rendering-conditioned video generation ideas.

Because SPMem and Context-as-Memory are not open-sourced, the authors reimplement both baselines themselves; while reasonable, this raises some risk of implementation/tuning asymmetry favoring the proposed method, and no confidence intervals, multiple-seed results, or statistical significance are reported for the main quantitative comparisons.

The main quantitative benchmark (Table 1) only evaluates a 49-frame partial-revisit setting; the more interesting long-horizon claims (hundreds to thousands of frames) are supported mainly by qualitative figures and a single stress-test comparison against SPMem only, without other baselines, limiting the strength of the long-horizon consistency claims made in the abstract/introduction.

The single-anchor variant (K=1) of AnchorWeave already outperforms nearly all baselines in Table 1, suggesting a large share of the improvement comes from the coverage-driven retrieval strategy itself rather than the multi-anchor weaving controller; the marginal benefit of the full multi-anchor design over K=1 is comparatively modest, which somewhat undercuts the emphasis placed on the weaving controller as a central contribution.

The dynamic out-of-sight memory extension (Fig. 12) is explicitly described as only "sketched"/conceptual and not actually implemented or evaluated, yet it is presented as supporting evidence for the framework's extensibility to dynamic worlds — this weakens the rigor of that claim.

Reflective/view-dependent surfaces are identified as a clear failure mode inherent to any point-cloud-based static memory representation; given how common such surfaces are in real environments (mirrors, glass, water), this is a non-trivial limitation that is acknowledged but not analyzed quantitatively (e.g., frequency/impact across the benchmark).

No user study is conducted; perceptual quality and spatial consistency claims rely solely on automatic metrics (PSNR/SSIM/VBench dimensions), which are known to be imperfect proxies for human-perceived long-horizon world consistency.

Storage/memory growth of the per-frame local point-cloud bank over very long trajectories is not analyzed (only rendering/retrieval runtime is benchmarked), leaving open how the approach scales in memory footprint for arbitrarily long exploration.

No explicit statement on code/data/model release is provided beyond an anonymized webpage with qualitative videos, which leaves some uncertainty about reproducibility of the full training/evaluation pipeline.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies a concrete and important failure mode of prior global-3D-memory video generation methods (cross-view misalignment accumulating into ghosting/hallucination artifacts) and proposes a targeted fix.

The core idea—replacing a single fused global memory with multiple per-frame local geometric memories reconciled via a learned multi-anchor weaving controller—is intuitive, technically sound, and directly addresses the diagnosed failure mode rather than being an incremental architectural tweak without justification.

Extensive quantitative comparison against a wide range of relevant, recent baselines (Gen3C, SEVA, ViewCrafter, TrajCrafter, EPiC, Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on two datasets (RealEstate10K, DL3DV), with consistent improvements in both reconstruction fidelity (PSNR/SSIM) and VBench-style perceptual metrics.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice: local vs. global memory (Table 2), pose-guided fusion vs. naive averaging (Fig. 5a), joint vs. separate attention (Fig. 5b), and number of retrieved anchors (Table 3), each supported by both quantitative results and clear qualitative visualizations.

Strong appendix material substantially strengthens the submission: a long-horizon stress test to 2400 frames showing AnchorWeave remains stable while the global-memory baseline (SPMem) degrades and eventually runs out of memory; efficiency/scaling analysis showing favorable runtime growth versus global point-cloud fusion; camera-controllability comparison (rotation/translation error) versus baselines; and demonstrations of generalization to dynamic content via masking and 360° panoramic consistency.

Honest and specific limitations/failure-mode discussion (reflective surfaces, pose drift over very long horizons, dependency on the backbone/3D estimator), which strengthens rather than undermines the paper's credibility.

Method is demonstrated on two different DiT backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B), suggesting the approach is not tied to one specific generator and supporting reproducibility with reasonably detailed implementation/training details and pseudocode for the retrieval algorithm.
weaknesses: The comparison methods Context-as-Memory and SPMem are not open-sourced and had to be reimplemented by the authors on the same backbone/data; while reasonably documented, this introduces some risk of unintentional reimplementation bias favoring the proposed method that independent verification cannot rule out.

Quantitative evaluation of dynamic-content handling (masking moving objects out of the static memory) is only qualitative (Figs. 11-12); no metrics are reported to substantiate robustness in dynamic scenes, despite this being highlighted as a capability.

Absolute reconstruction fidelity remains fairly modest (PSNR in the ~19-21 dB range even for the proposed method), indicating a still-large gap to ground truth under the partial-revisit evaluation protocol; the paper could better contextualize how far from "solved" this problem remains.

The method depends on an off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction/pose model (TTT3R) whose failure modes (e.g., on out-of-distribution or reflective scenes) directly propagate into generation quality; while acknowledged in limitations, the sensitivity of the overall pipeline to different or weaker 3D estimators is not empirically studied.

Several important hyperparameters (chunk length D, memory update frequency, retrieval stopping criteria) are fixed by design choice with limited sensitivity analysis beyond the number of retrieved anchors K, leaving open questions about robustness to these settings.
No human/user study is included to corroborate the automated VBench-style perceptual metrics, which is a common limitation but relevant given the visual-quality claims made.
